questions.text_verbatim: (a) Describe the structure of IMO. Specify the responsibilities and work done by the Assembly, the Council and various main committees. What role do the sub-committees perform in supporting the main committees? (b) Define a convention. Explain the differences in international instruments such as Convention, Protocol, Code and Resolution. Give at least one example of each.
questions.understand_first: This question is not testing whether you can list acronyms. It is testing whether you understand that IMO separates POLICY (Assembly, Council) from TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT (committees, sub-committees), and that in the instrument hierarchy the binding force comes from the treaty route rather than from what the document is called.

blocks.h: 1. What IMO is, and the organs that do the work

blocks.p: The International Maritime Organization is the specialised agency of the United Nations responsible for the safety and security of shipping and for the prevention of pollution from ships. It works through a two-tier governing structure - an Assembly and a Council - together with five main committees supported by seven sub-committees, all served by a permanent Secretariat headed by the Secretary-General. The governing organs decide policy, budget and membership questions; the technical output that reaches a ship comes almost entirely from the committees.

ul: The highest governing body. All Member States sit in it.
Meets in regular session once every two years.
Approves the work programme and votes the budget, and determines the financial arrangements.
Elects the Council.
Receives the reports of the Council and the committees, and adopts Assembly resolutions - recommendations, guidelines and codes.
Example of its output: resolution A.1207(34), the HSSC Survey Guidelines 2025, adopted by the 34th Assembly on 3 December 2025.

40 Members, elected by the Assembly for a two-year term, in three categories: (a) ten States with the largest interest in providing international shipping services; (b) ten States with the largest interest in international seaborne trade; (c) twenty States elected to secure geographical representation of all major areas.

Between Assembly sessions it performs all the functions of the Assembly, except the function of making recommendations to Governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention, which the Assembly reserves to itself.
Supervises the work of the Organization and co-ordinates the activities of the organs.
Considers the draft work programme and budget and submits them to the Assembly with its comments.
Appoints the Secretary-General, subject to Assembly approval.

blocks.h: 4. The five main committees and what each owns

rows: The highest technical body. All matters of navigational safety, construction and equipment, manning from a safety standpoint, casualty investigation, salvage and rescue
Prevention and control of pollution from ships - MARPOL and its amendments, ballast water, anti-fouling, and greenhouse-gas measures
Any legal matter within the scope of the Organization - liability and compensation conventions in particular
Implementation of the Organization's technical assistance work, particularly for developing States
Elimination of unnecessary formalities and red tape in international shipping - the FAL Convention

blocks.p: All five are open to all Member States. MSC and MEPC are the two that adopt amendments to the mandatory instruments.

blocks.h: 5. The seven sub-committees, and the role they perform

blocks.p: The sub-committees are HTW (Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping), III (Implementation of IMO Instruments), NCSR (Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue), PPR (Pollution Prevention and Response), SDC (Ship Design and Construction), SSE (Ship Systems and Equipment) and CCC (Carriage of Cargoes and Containers).

Their role in supporting the main committees is preparatory and technical. A committee meets for a week or so and cannot itself draft detailed regulation, so it remits the work to the sub-committee with the relevant expertise. The sub-committee develops the draft text, guidelines or unified interpretation, resolves the technical argument, and reports back to its parent committee - MSC, MEPC, or both. A sub-committee adopts nothing. It prepares; the parent committee approves; the committee or the Assembly adopts. That division is what keeps technical depth and treaty-making authority in different hands.

A convention is a formal, legally binding treaty between States. It is negotiated and adopted at a diplomatic conference or by the Assembly, is then opened for signature, ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, and enters into force only when the conditions written into the convention itself are satisfied - typically a stated number of Contracting States representing a stated share of world tonnage. It binds only those States that have become party to it. Example: the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974.

blocks.h: 7. Protocol, Code and Resolution - how each differs, with examples

rows: A separate treaty instrument that amends, supplements or modifies a parent convention, adopted where the change is too large for the ordinary amendment procedure. A State may have to be party to both
The 1978 and 1997 Protocols to MARPOL; the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Lines Convention, which introduced the harmonized system of survey and certification
A detailed technical instrument. Of itself it is recommendatory; it becomes mandatory only when a convention makes it so. Mandatory status is a property of the route, not of the word 'Code'
The ISM Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX. Contrast the Intact Stability Code Part B, which remains recommendatory

The formal decision of the Assembly or of a committee. It is the vehicle by which an instrument is adopted, or by which guidance is issued. A resolution is recommendatory unless what it carries has been made mandatory
A.1207(34) - recommendatory survey guidelines. Contrast MEPC.328(76), a resolution adopting the revised MARPOL Annex VI, which is mandatory because MARPOL makes it so

blocks.p: The marks in limb (a) are in the function columns, not the names. Anyone can write 'MSC, MEPC, Legal, TC, FAL'; the mark comes from saying what each one is for. The examiner has also asked one narrow question inside limb (a) - what role the sub-committees play in supporting the main committees - and it is the part most candidates leave out. Step 5 answers it explicitly and states the negative as well as the positive: a sub-committee has no adoption power.
Limb (b) is worth the same eight marks and is far quicker to write, so write it properly. A three-column table with an example in each row banks the marks in about a third of the time limb (a) takes.

blocks.h: The one idea that makes limb (b) easy

blocks.p: Candidates try to memorise which instruments are 'mandatory'. That is the wrong model and it does not survive a follow-up question. The right model is: obligation comes from the treaty route, not from the label. A Code is a container of technical text. It becomes binding when a convention to which a State is party says it is binding. That is why the ISM Code binds - SOLAS chapter IX says so - and why an identically-titled 'Code' with no such hook does not.

ul: Naming only MSC and MEPC as the 'main committees'. There are five, and the question says 'various main committees'.
Saying the Assembly meets annually. It meets in regular session every two years.
Describing the sub-committees as if they adopt regulation. They do not.
Writing that a Code is 'always mandatory' or 'always recommendatory'. Neither is true.
Confusing a Protocol with an amendment. An ordinary amendment is adopted under the convention's own amendment article; a Protocol is a separate treaty.
Giving no examples in limb (b) when the question expressly asks for at least one of each - that is a straight loss of marks for something the candidate already knows.

The Council's size. An amendment to enlarge the Council from 40 to 52 was adopted in December 2021 but requires acceptance by two thirds of Members. IMO's own convention page still records it as not yet in force (checked 21 September 2026). Write 40, and if the enlargement is mentioned, mention it as an amendment adopted but not in force.
The Secretary-General. Arsenio Dominguez has held office since 1 January 2024, for a four-year term. Naming his predecessor dates the script badly.
Being asked in the oral 'so is the ISM Code a convention?' The answer is no - it is a Code given mandatory force by SOLAS chapter IX.
Being asked which organ adopts MARPOL amendments. MEPC does, by resolution, under the MARPOL amendment article - not the Assembly.
Which committee would deal with a new requirement for lifeboat release gear? MSC, remitted to SSE.
Who adopted the revised MARPOL Annex VI? MEPC, by resolution MEPC.328(76).
What is the difference between adoption and entry into force? Adoption is the decision to make the text; entry into force is when it starts to bind, on the conditions the instrument itself sets.
Name a Code that is not mandatory. Part B of the Intact Stability Code.
Who appoints the Secretary-General? The Council, subject to Assembly approval.

blocks.p: For limb (a) the shape is top down: Assembly (everyone, every two years) - Council (40, executive) - Committees (five, technical) - Sub-committees (seven, preparatory) - Secretariat. For the five committees use two engines and three others: MSC and MEPC do the mandatory work; Legal, TC and FAL do the rest. For limb (b), one sentence: a Convention binds, a Protocol changes what binds, a Code supplies the detail, a Resolution is how the decision was taken.

blocks.p: The organs, their functions and the committee and sub-committee lists are stable and were re-confirmed for September 2026. The one genuinely date-sensitive item is the Council's size: the enlargement to 52 was adopted in December 2021 and was still not in force on 21 September 2026, so 40 remains correct; a later sitting must re-check it. The Secretary-General's identity is likewise sitting-specific. Neither the Convention on the IMO nor any consolidated IMO structural publication is held in the MIW corpus, so limb (a)'s institutional facts rest on the Organization's own published account - authoritative secondary, and recorded as such.

blocks.h: 1. The background - the gap the Convention was written to close

blocks.p: By the late 1990s the international regime for oil pollution was substantial but narrow. The 1992 CLC, backed by the 1992 Fund, applied only to persistent oil carried as cargo in bulk by a tanker. It said nothing about the far more common case of a bulk carrier, container ship or car carrier spilling its own fuel. A large modern non-tanker may carry several thousand tonnes of heavy fuel oil - more than the entire cargo of a small tanker - and a claimant faced with such a spill had no dedicated convention, no guaranteed insurer to sue and no certainty of recovery. The International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage was adopted on 23 March 2001 and entered into force on 21 November 2008 to close exactly that gap.

blocks.h: 2. Its relevance - where it sits in the liability architecture

blocks.p: Its relevance is that it completes the map. Taken with CLC and the Fund for tanker cargo, and the HNS Convention for hazardous and noxious substances, the Bunkers Convention brings the fuel of essentially the whole world fleet inside a regime of strict liability, compulsory insurance and direct action against the insurer. It applies to pollution damage in the territory, territorial sea and exclusive economic zone of a State Party, and to preventive measures wherever taken. Its structural weakness, dealt with at step 7, is that it stops there: it creates no limitation fund of its own and no second tier of compensation.

Bunkers article 1.9 defines pollution damage as loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, provided that compensation for impairment of the environment other than loss of profit from that impairment is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and it includes the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

Against CLC 92: the definition is deliberately the same in substance. The drafters copied the CLC formula so that the two regimes would be interpreted consistently and no claimant would be better or worse off according to which convention applied. The difference lies not in what pollution damage means but in which oil, from which ship, triggers it.

Bunkers article 1.5: any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. Three features matter. It expressly catches lubricating oil, which candidates routinely forget. It catches residues, so sludge and tank washings are within it. And unlike CLC it is not limited to persistent oil - a marine gas oil spill is bunker oil for these purposes.

Against CLC 92: CLC applies to persistent hydrocarbon mineral oil - crude, fuel oil, heavy diesel, lubricating oil - carried as cargo, and to such oil in the bunkers of a ship carrying that cargo. So the same drum of lubricating oil is CLC oil in a laden tanker's bunkers and Bunkers Convention oil in a bulk carrier's sump.

Bunkers article 8. Rights to compensation are extinguished unless an action is brought within three years from the date the damage occurred. In no case may an action be brought more than six years from the date of the incident which caused the damage. Where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six-year period runs from the date of the first occurrence.

Against CLC 92: substantially identical - CLC article VIII sets the same three-year and six-year periods on the same terms. This is one of the places where the drafters deliberately mirrored CLC. Note the wording: the right is extinguished, not merely barred, so it cannot be revived.
Three different things are commonly called exclusions and the answer should separate them:

ol: Excluded damage - the CLC carve-out. Article 4.1: the Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable under it. This is the hinge that stops the two regimes overlapping. A laden tanker's bunker spill is a CLC matter, not a Bunkers matter.
Excluded ships. Article 4.2: it does not apply to warships, naval auxiliaries or other State-owned or operated ships used on government non-commercial service, unless a State Party decides otherwise.

The shipowner's defences - strictly not exclusions at all but a different route to no liability. Under article 3.3 the shipowner is not liable if the damage resulted from an act of war, hostilities, civil war, insurrection or a natural phenomenon of an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible character; was wholly caused by a third party's act or omission done with intent to cause damage; or was wholly caused by the negligence or wrongful act of a Government or authority responsible for maintaining lights or other navigational aids. Contributory fault of the claimant may also reduce or exonerate.

blocks.p: Against CLC 92: the defences are the same three, in the same terms. The excluded-ship provision is likewise mirrored. The CLC carve-out itself has no CLC equivalent, because CLC is the senior regime.

blocks.h: 7. How the Bunker Convention differs from CLC 92, taken together

rows: 'Shipowner' defined widely - registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally
No limit of its own. Article 6 preserves the right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, in practice the LLMC
Its own tonnage-based limits in article V
Registered owner of a ship over 1,000 GT
Ship carrying more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil as cargo

blocks.p: The practical consequence of rows three and four is the point worth making last: where a very large bunker spill exhausts the LLMC limit, there is nothing behind it. That is the principal criticism of the regime.

The printed question gives you your own headings - (a), (b), (c), (d) - so the structure is free. The mark is lost in a different way: by defining the four terms and never doing the comparison the stem asks for. Every one of steps 3 to 6 therefore ends with an explicit 'Against CLC 92' sentence. That single habit converts a half answer into a full one.

Step 7 exists because the most important difference does not live under any of the four definitions. It is structural - who is liable, what limit applies, and what stands behind it. Putting it in a table at the end banks a large number of comparison marks quickly.

CLC is a cargo regime. Bunkers is a fuel regime. Everything else follows. CLC could afford exclusive channelling to the registered owner and a dedicated fund because the industry paying for the fund - oil receivers - is identifiable and finite. There is no equivalent constituency to levy for bunkers, so the Bunkers Convention got neither a fund nor its own limit, and had to widen the definition of 'shipowner' instead so that a claimant has more than one solvent defendant.

ul: Omitting lubricating oil from the definition of bunker oil. It is expressly in the text.
Saying bunker oil must be persistent. It need not be - that is a CLC requirement, not a Bunkers one.
Writing that liability is channelled to the registered owner. That is CLC. Under Bunkers it reaches the bareboat charterer, manager and operator as well.
Saying the Bunkers Convention has its own limits of liability. It does not - it borrows the LLMC.
Confusing the six-year long stop with the three-year period, or giving only one of the two.
Treating the shipowner's defences as if they were the article 4 exclusions. They are separate provisions doing separate work.
Forgetting the CLC carve-out - it is the single most important exclusion and the one that makes the system coherent.

'Whether or not compensation is payable under CLC.' Those words in article 4.1 matter. Even where the CLC claim fails, the Bunkers Convention does not step in. The claimant does not get a second bite.
The insurance thresholds are different units. Bunkers is 1,000 GT, a tonnage of the ship. CLC is 2,000 tonnes of oil carried, a quantity of cargo. Candidates frequently swap them.
'Extinguished', not 'barred'. The right ceases to exist.
Being asked what happens after the LLMC limit is exhausted on a bunker spill. The honest answer is that the convention regime provides nothing further.
Being asked whether the Bunkers Convention applies on the high seas. It applies to pollution damage in the territory, territorial sea and EEZ - but to preventive measures wherever taken.
A laden tanker spills bunkers. Which convention? CLC - and Bunkers is excluded by article 4.1.
A container ship spills lube oil. Which convention? Bunkers - lubricating oil is expressly within article 1.5.
Who can the claimant sue? Any of the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager or operator, jointly and severally; and the insurer directly.
Why is there no bunker fund? There is no identifiable cargo-receiving industry to levy, as there is for oil under the Fund Convention.

Is India a party to the Bunker Convention? No - the depositary's Status of IMO Treaties at 26 August 2026 records no Indian accession to BUNKERS 2001. She is a Party to CLC 1992 (accession 15 November 1999, in force for India 15 November 2000). Write the answer on the Convention either way - the question asks about the Convention.

Is India a Party to the Bunker Convention at this sitting? No. The depositary's Status of IMO Treaties at 26 August 2026 records no Indian accession to BUNKERS 2001 - the list runs Hungary, then Indonesia (re-read for this candidate on 21 September 2026). India is a Party to CLC 1992: accession 15 November 1999, in force for India 15 November 2000.

Domestic law (context, not what the question asks): the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 contains a chapter titled 'Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage', and the whole Act has been in force since 15 March 2026 (S.O. 1244(E)). Its section numbers are not quoted here because they were not re-read for this candidate.

Does an Indian certificate or insurance requirement prove India is a Party? No, and this is the trap. A State may enact the substance of a Convention in its own law without ever acceding to it. Party status is proved from the depositary's status list, never from domestic legislation.

blocks.p: Two openers, four definitions, one table: 2-4-1. For the definitions use P-B-T-E - Pollution damage, Bunker oil, Time limits, Exclusions - which is the printed order, so nothing extra to remember. For the numbers, 3 and 6 are the time limits, 1,000 is Bunkers insurance in GT and 2,000 is CLC insurance in tonnes of cargo.

rows: Exclusions - CLC damage and State ships
Compulsory insurance over 1,000 GT, direct action

No CLC monetary limitation figure is quoted anywhere in this answer - those figures are amendable by tacit acceptance, and quoting a superseded number would be worse than omitting it. India's party status is not asserted, because the question is about the Conventions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Bunker Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Background - the gap. 2 Relevance - where it sits. 3 (a) Pollution damage. 4 (b) Bunker oil. 5 (c) Time limits. 6 (d) Exclusions. 7 The structural differences from CLC 92 in a table.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 3 to 6 are the printed limbs. Step 7 carries the differences that do not belong under any one definition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define bunker oil under the 2001 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Any hydrocarbon mineral oil, including lubricating oil, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. It is not confined to persistent oil.
retrieval_cards.why: Lubricating oil and residues are the two elements most often omitted, and 'need not be persistent' is the contrast with CLC.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define pollution damage under the 2001 Convention.
retrieval_cards.answer: Loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of bunker oil, provided that compensation for environmental impairment other than loss of profit is limited to the costs of reasonable measures of reinstatement actually undertaken or to be undertaken; and the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.
retrieval_cards.why: The proviso is the marks-bearing part - it is what stops open-ended environmental claims.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the time limits for claims, and what happens on a series of occurrences?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rights are extinguished unless action is brought within three years from the date the damage occurred, and in no case more than six years from the date of the incident. Where the incident consists of a series of occurrences, the six-year period runs from the date of the first occurrence.
retrieval_cards.why: Two periods, not one, plus the series rule. CLC article VIII is the same.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the exclusions, and how do they differ from the shipowner's defences?
retrieval_cards.answer: Exclusions: pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable under it; and warships, naval auxiliaries and State ships on government non-commercial service. The defences are separate - act of war or exceptional natural phenomenon, damage wholly caused by a third party intending damage, or wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids.
retrieval_cards.why: Three different things get called 'exclusions'. Separating them is what a good answer does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the four structural differences between the Bunkers Convention and CLC 92.
retrieval_cards.answer: Who is liable - Bunkers reaches registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally; CLC channels exclusively to the registered owner. Limitation - Bunkers has none of its own and preserves the LLMC; CLC has its own limits. Second tier - Bunkers has no fund; CLC has the 1992 Fund and Supplementary Fund. Insurance threshold - over 1,000 GT against more than 2,000 tonnes of oil as cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the comparison the stem actually asks for and the largest single block of marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A laden tanker spills its own bunkers. Which convention applies?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC 92. Bunkers article 4.1 excludes pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is actually payable under it - so the claimant cannot fall back on the Bunkers Convention if the CLC claim fails.
retrieval_cards.why: The classic viva question, and the 'whether or not payable' wording is the sting.

quick_revision.recall_15s: CLC covers persistent oil as CARGO in a tanker; Bunkers covers the FUEL of every other ship. Adopted 2001, in force 21 November 2008. Pollution damage - same formula as CLC. Bunker oil - any hydrocarbon mineral oil including LUBRICATING OIL and residues, need not be persistent. Time limits - 3 years from damage, 6-year long stop from the incident. Exclusions - CLC damage, warships and State non-commercial ships. The big structural difference: wide shipowner definition, NO own limit (borrows the LLMC), NO fund.
critical_numbers: Time bar: 3 years from damage; 6 years long stop from the incident
Compulsory insurance: more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil as cargo (CLC)
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Bunkers Convention article 4.1 - the Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in the CLC, whether or not compensation is payable under it. That carve-out is what keeps the two regimes from overlapping.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing that liability is channelled exclusively to the registered owner. That is CLC. Under Bunkers article 1.3 'shipowner' includes the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager AND operator, jointly and severally. The second trap is omitting lubricating oil from the bunker oil definition.

questions.text_verbatim: Optimization of hull Forms is recognized as means to improve energy efficiency of ships. Discuss scope and impact of optimization of the following in improving energy efficiency of ships: (a) Forebody optimization (b) Aft-body optimization (c) Twin Skeg Design
questions.understand_first: The forebody and the aftbody are not doing the same job. The forebody is shaped to reduce resistance - principally wave-making. The aftbody is shaped to deliver good water to the propeller. Twin skeg is an aftbody decision, taken when restricted draught will not let a single propeller be big enough. If you hold that, you can reason out most of this answer rather than recall it.
questions.memory_cue: Two framing steps (1, 2), then the three printed items in printed order (3, 4, 5), then limits (6). Under each of 3, 4 and 5 write Scope then Impact.

blocks.h: 1. Why the hull form governs the power the ship needs

blocks.p: Total resistance divides into frictional resistance, which depends on wetted surface area and hull roughness; wave-making resistance, the energy left behind in the wave system; and viscous pressure or form resistance, arising from the way the flow separates and thickens around the hull. For a full-form, relatively slow merchant ship friction dominates, but wave-making and form resistance are the components the designer can actually change by reshaping the hull.

Hull form also sets the second term in the propulsion equation. Delivered power is resistance times speed divided by the propulsive coefficient, and the hull efficiency element of that coefficient - the relationship between wake fraction and thrust deduction - is a direct product of the aftbody shape. The hull therefore appears on both sides of the problem, which is why it is the largest single design lever available.

blocks.h: 2. How hull form optimisation is done, and what changed

blocks.p: The modern method is parametric hull modelling coupled to computational fluid dynamics. The hull is described by a set of driving parameters, thousands of variants are generated and evaluated by CFD - potential flow for wave making, viscous RANS solvers for the wake field - and the promising forms are verified by model tank testing. CFD proposes; the tank still confirms.

The decisive change is what the hull is optimised for. Historically a hull was optimised at one design speed and one design draught. Since slow steaming became normal, ships spend their lives away from that point. Optimisation is now carried out over a matrix of speeds and draughts weighted by the ship's real operating profile, which is also why retrofit optimisation of existing ships is worthwhile - many were shaped for a speed they will never see again.
Sketch - where each of the three measures acts; generic, not to scale, no saving quantified. Tap the sketch to open it full size.

Scope. The bulbous bow - its volume, length, shape and vertical position; the waterline entrance angle; the fairing of the forward shoulder; and the stem profile. On existing ships this is the classic bow retrofit: the bulb is cut off and replaced, or removed altogether in favour of a straight stem.

Impact. The forebody governs the wave-making component. A bulb works by generating a wave system in antiphase with the bow wave so that the two partially cancel - but that cancellation is tuned to a particular speed and draught, and off that point the bulb can add resistance rather than remove it. A bulb designed for a laden design speed may be actively harmful in ballast or at slow steaming speed. Reshaping also improves added resistance in waves, which matters because the ship meets real seas rather than calm water, and improves ballast-condition performance where the old bulb sat near the surface.
Scope. The run of the buttock lines, the choice between U-form and V-form sections, the stern bulb, the shaft bossing and skeg arrangement, and the propeller aperture and tip clearances.

Impact. The aftbody's real job is not resistance but the quality of the water delivered to the propeller. A full stern produces a thick, distorted boundary layer, so each blade passes through a strongly varying inflow once per revolution. That non-uniform wake causes cavitation, pressure pulses, hull vibration and erosion, and lowers propulsive efficiency. Optimisation aims at a more uniform, better organised wake field, which allows a higher blade loading without cavitation and improves the hull efficiency term. There is a genuine trade-off: a wake that is too uniform loses some of the wake gain that makes a single-screw ship efficient in the first place.

Keep the distinction clear. Pre-swirl ducts, stators, fins and boss cap fins are energy saving devices bolted to the hull. They exploit a poor wake; they are not aftbody form optimisation, and an answer that treats them as the same thing has missed what the question asked.

Scope. Two separate skegs, each carrying its own shaft line and propeller, in place of a single centreline screw. It suits ships with high block coefficient, large beam and restricted draught, and high installed power - large LNG carriers, ro-ro and car carriers, and bulkers and tankers on draught-limited trades.

Impact - what it buys. On a shallow-draught ship, propeller diameter is the binding constraint. Two smaller propellers permit a larger total disc area and lower revolutions than one propeller squeezed under a flat stern, and open-water efficiency improves accordingly. Each propeller sits in cleaner, more uniform inflow outboard of the centreline, so cavitation and vibration fall. The hull can carry a fuller midbody without the usual penalty, protecting cargo capacity. Redundancy is a real operational benefit.

Impact - what it costs. Two skegs add wetted surface area, and therefore frictional resistance, which on a friction-dominated hull is a significant debit. Two shafts, sterntubes, bearings and sets of machinery raise capital cost and maintenance. Twin skeg is therefore a net gain only where the propulsive efficiency benefit outweighs the added friction - which is precisely the high-block, restricted-draught, high-power case.

blocks.h: 6. What limits the gains, and where they are measured

blocks.p: The gains are design-specific and do not simply add: improving the wake field alters the flow the bulb sees, so the hull must be optimised as a whole. Because hull form is a design property it is one of the few genuine levers on attained EEDI for a newbuilding and on attained EEXI for an existing ship, both under MARPOL Annex VI. In service the benefit appears as reduced fuel per unit of transport work and therefore in the operational carbon intensity indicator, in force since 1 January 2023 - which is the commercial reason the subject has become urgent again.

The question names three items and asks for scope and impact of each. The highest-scoring habit on this question is trivially simple: write the words Scope and Impact as sub-labels under each of steps 3, 4 and 5. It guarantees that both halves of the question are answered for all three items, and it makes the examiner's marking obvious.

Steps 1 and 2 are not padding. Without the resistance breakdown you cannot explain why the forebody and aftbody are optimised for different objectives, which is the single insight that separates a good answer from a list.

Forward and aft are solving different problems. The forebody fights resistance. The aftbody feeds the propeller. Almost every mark on this question can be reasoned out from that one sentence: it explains why bulb design is speed- and draught-sensitive, why aftbody work is discussed in terms of wake and cavitation rather than drag, and why twin skeg - which is an aftbody decision - is justified by propeller diameter and inflow rather than by reduced resistance.

ul: Treating a bulbous bow as always beneficial. It is tuned to a design point and can add resistance off it.
Discussing ducts, stators and fins as 'aftbody optimisation'. They are appendages.
Claiming twin skeg reduces resistance. It increases wetted surface and frictional resistance; the gain is in propulsive efficiency.
Giving a single percentage saving for each measure as though it were a constant. It is design-specific.
Forgetting that hull form optimisation is now done for an operating profile, which is the whole reason retrofits are viable.
Answering only 'scope' and never 'impact', or the reverse.
Why remove a bulbous bow? Because the ship no longer runs at the speed and draught the bulb was tuned for. This is the classic follow-up and catches candidates who learned that bulbs are simply good.
Is a perfectly uniform wake ideal? No. Some wake non-uniformity is what gives a single-screw ship its wake gain; the aim is a well-organised wake, not a flat one.
Twin skeg on a fine-form fast ship? Poor choice - friction dominates the debit and there is no draught constraint to justify it.
Being asked which of EEDI, EEXI and CII hull form affects. All three, but EEDI and EEXI are design/technical indices while CII is operational.
Being asked to quantify. Decline to invent a number and explain what it depends on - ship type, operating profile, and how far the existing form is from its optimum.
Name the components of ship resistance and say which dominates on a loaded bulk carrier. Frictional.
What is thrust deduction, and why does the aftbody affect it? The propeller lowers pressure ahead of itself and increases hull resistance; the stern shape governs how strongly.
How is a candidate hull verified before build? CFD screening, then model tank test.
Why do twin skeg ships tend to be LNG carriers and car carriers? Large beam, restricted draught, high power, and cargo capacity that must not be sacrificed.
What is added resistance in waves and why is it now designed for? Real seaway resistance above calm-water; it is now part of the operating-profile optimisation.

blocks.p: Two jobs, three items. Forward fights resistance; aft feeds the propeller; twin skeg is an aft decision driven by draught. Then for each of the three, the same two words: Scope, Impact. For the physics use F-W-V: Frictional, Wave-making, Viscous pressure.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of what can be quantified

blocks.p: This is a hydrodynamics and design question and the answer is written as such. No numeric percentage saving is quoted anywhere for any of the three measures. That is deliberate: published gains for bow retrofits, aftbody reshaping and twin skeg arrangements vary by ship type, by how far the existing form sits from its optimum, and by the operating profile assumed, and a single figure presented as general would be false precision. The production protocol requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than invented. The regulatory statements at step 6 hold at September 2026: EEXI and the operational CII have been in force since 1 January 2023. The reading of 'Twin Skeg Design' as a twin-screw arrangement is stated in the answer rather than assumed silently.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What different objective does the forebody serve compared with the aftbody?
retrieval_cards.answer: The forebody is shaped to reduce resistance, principally the wave-making component. The aftbody is shaped to deliver a uniform, well-organised wake to the propeller, governing cavitation, pressure pulses, vibration and the hull efficiency term of the propulsive coefficient.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why would an owner cut off and replace a bulbous bow?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a bulb cancels the bow wave only at the speed and draught it was tuned for. After slow steaming or a change of trade the ship no longer operates there, and the bulb may be adding resistance rather than removing it. Retrofit re-tunes the forebody to the real operating profile.
retrieval_cards.why: The classic follow-up, and it tests whether the candidate understands the mechanism rather than the slogan.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a twin skeg arrangement and which ships suit it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two separate skegs each carrying its own shaft and propeller instead of a single centreline screw. It suits high block coefficient, large beam, restricted draught and high installed power - large LNG carriers, ro-ro and car carriers, and draught-limited bulkers and tankers.
retrieval_cards.why: Scope for item (iii); the ship types are the quickest way to show you understand why.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a twin skeg hull have lower resistance than a single screw hull?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Two skegs add wetted surface and therefore frictional resistance. The benefit is propulsive - larger total propeller disc area at lower revolutions, and cleaner inflow to each propeller - and it outweighs the friction penalty only on high-block, draught-restricted, high-power ships.
retrieval_cards.why: The most common wrong statement made about twin skeg.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are pre-swirl ducts and stators part of aftbody optimisation?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. They are energy saving devices - appendages fitted to the hull that exploit the existing wake. Aftbody optimisation means changing the shape of the hull itself: buttock lines, section form, stern bulb, bossings and propeller clearances.
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks about hull form; conflating form with appendages loses the point of item (ii).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MARPOL Annex VI measures does hull form bear on, and how?
retrieval_cards.answer: Hull form is a design property, so it bears directly on attained EEDI for a newbuilding (chapter 4, regulation 22) and attained EEXI for an existing ship (regulation 23). In service the reduced fuel per unit transport work shows in the operational carbon intensity indicator (regulation 28). EEXI and CII were both in force from 1 January 2023.
retrieval_cards.why: Step 6, and the commercial reason the subject matters.

questions.text_verbatim: With specific reference to any make, sketch and describe the Cylinder Lubricating System used in new generation marine diesel engines. How will you effect the optimum cylinder oil feed with varying sulphur content of fuel oil.
questions.understand_first: There are two variables, not one. The oil's BASE NUMBER is how much alkali each drop carries; the FEED RATE is how many drops arrive. What the liner actually needs is alkali per unit of sulphur burnt, which is the product of the two. On a modern engine the two are even set by different equipment: the supply system (switching or mixing) decides which oil reaches the lubricator, and the lubricator control decides how much of it is injected. Every operating decision in the second half of this answer follows from that product.

blocks.p: Core examination answer - steps 1 to 7. Write this in the examination. Step 8 is a separately labelled technical extension; the maker's published values and the WinGD alternative are in the Study Guide.

blocks.h: 1. What the cylinder oil must do, and why it is once-through

blocks.p: In a two-stroke crosshead engine the cylinder oil is separate from the system oil. It maintains the oil film between rings and liner, neutralises the acid formed from the fuel's sulphur, keeps the ring pack and piston crown clean, helps the rings seal, and carries debris down to the scavenge space. It is a total-loss (once-through) system: every drop is burnt or scraped down and none returns. The quantity injected is therefore both a running cost and the principal wear variable - which is why the question asks how to optimise it.

blocks.h: 2. The system layout - what the sketch must show

blocks.p: Naming a make, as the question requires: the Everllence (formerly MAN Energy Solutions) B&W G95ME-C10.5-GI, a current electronically controlled two-stroke engine with the maker's Alpha cylinder lubrication system. Sketch the path of the oil and label it:

ol: Low-BN and high-BN cylinder oil storage/service tanks, kept separate, feeding by gravity.

ACOS2 switching valve - the maker's standard: an air-operated three-way valve, controlled by the engine control system, that selects one oil and fails safe to the high-BN oil. (The ACOM Mk III mixing unit is the option - step 8.) Sketch D1 shows the valve on the ship side, ahead of one heating tank, with a single engine inlet; for GI engines the maker also shows it on the engine, behind separate low-BN and high-BN inlets - see D3.
Filter in the supply line.
Cylinder oil heating tank with heater and low-level alarm, sited above the engine inlet.
Insulated, electrically heat-traced pipe to the engine inlet and the main pipe along the engine, with an open/closed supply valve on the branch to each lubricator.

Alpha lubricator on each cylinder's hydraulic cylinder unit (HCU) - the HCU is supplied with the engine's 300 bar hydraulic (system) oil; the lubricator's own small multi-piston pumps meter the cylinder oil and inject it, each stroke triggered by a solenoid valve (a proportional valve on the Alpha Mk 2).
Lubricating quills round the liner, each with a non-return valve - the number depends on the engine type.

Cylinder Control Unit (CCU) for each cylinder, using engine speed and fuel index, with the settings and the fuel-sulphur figure entered on the operating panel, and a feedback sensor on the lubricator.
Scavenge space and piston-underside drain, from which scrape-down samples are drawn.

blocks.h: 3. How the dose is timed and controlled

blocks.p: Unlike the old mechanical lubricator, the modern unit is electronically timed and independently metered. The control unit knows the crank position and injects a measured quantity through the non-return valves as the piston rings pass the quills on the upward stroke, so the oil goes into the ring pack rather than onto bare liner. Delivery is intermittent - for instance every 2, 4 or 8 revolutions - with the frequency set from engine speed and fuel index. Above a part-load breakpoint the feed follows engine load; below it, engine speed - so the dose can follow load, fuel sulphur and oil BN instead of a mechanical drive.

blocks.h: 4. Why sulphur content drives both the base number and the quantity

blocks.p: Fuel sulphur burns to sulphur dioxide and trioxide. Where the liner wall is below the acid dew point, water vapour condenses and the oxides dissolve in it as sulphuric acid on the liner. Unneutralised, this is cold corrosion - corrosive wear of liner and rings, very rapid in bad cases.

The oil carries an alkaline reserve (overbased detergent), measured as its Base Number (BN). Acid produced is proportional to the sulphur burnt - fuel consumption times sulphur percentage - so the alkali delivered must track the sulphur burnt. Alkali delivered is essentially BN times quantity: the engineer has two independent knobs, the grade and the feed rate. A high-BN oil at a low rate can match a lower-BN oil at a higher rate, which is why the grade is chosen before the rate is set.

blocks.h: 5. Setting the optimum feed rate in service

blocks.p: The procedure is: choose the grade, then set the quantity, then prove it.

ul: Select the BN grade for the fuel in use - a low-BN oil for fuel of up to 0.50% sulphur, a high-BN oil for high-sulphur fuel (ships with exhaust gas scrubbers). The switching valve puts the selected grade into the line.
Enter the sulphur figure from the bunker delivery note on the operating panel - the system cannot measure it.

Set the feed. On high-sulphur fuel the feed is proportional to load and to sulphur through the maker's feed-rate factor (formerly the ACC factor). On low-sulphur fuel the sulphur-proportional figure falls below the minimum, so the minimum feed-rate setting governs and is optimised from the cylinder condition.
Respect the maker's minimum feed rate - below it the film fails whatever the acid calculation says.

Optimise downward in small steps, only after confirming good cylinder condition and acceptable iron in the drain oil; hold and monitor between steps - never one large reduction, never during unstable load or running-in.

blocks.h: 6. How the engineer verifies the feed rate is right

rows: Scavenge drain (scrape-down) oil analysis from the piston underside drains

Residual BN: too high - alkali wasted, so the rate or grade can come down; too low - acid not fully neutralised. Iron: the wear rate; iron oxides point to corrosive wear, metallic iron to abrasive or adhesive wear. Laboratory analysis is the reference; onboard kits supplement it
Liner surface and running pattern, ring freedom and condition, crown and land deposits, scuffing or bore polishing - more often while the feed is being reduced
Closes the loop: confirms the long-term wear rate against the maker's expectation
Measured consumption against the control system's calculated figure; a shortfall means a lubricator fault, a leaking quill or a stuck non-return valve - raise the feed and investigate

blocks.h: 7. The traps - changeover, over-lubrication and the minimum

ul: Changing between high- and low-sulphur fuel without changing the setting. A high-BN oil left in use on low-sulphur fuel over-delivers alkali and builds deposits; a low-BN oil on high-sulphur fuel invites cold corrosion. Grade selection and the sulphur entry are part of the fuel changeover procedure.

Over-lubrication is not a safe error. Excess alkaline oil leaves hard calcium deposits on the top land and in the ring grooves, causes bore polishing that destroys the liner's oil-retaining honing, sticks rings and raises cost.
Never go below the maker's minimum, whatever a calculation suggests.
The low-sulphur trap. Little acid forms, but the oil is still needed for film strength and cleaning: use a suitable lower-BN grade at an adequate rate, not simply less of a high-BN oil.

blocks.h: 8. Technical extension - automatic grade supply, dual-fuel operation and maker differences

blocks.p: Technical extension - beyond the core answer. Credit-earning detail for a 'new generation' question; write it only after steps 1 to 7 are complete.
Automatic grade supply. Carrying two grades raises a practical question: how does the right one reach the lubricator? Everllence offers two supply systems:

ul: ACOS2 - automated cylinder oil switching (the standard system on most engines). It selects one of two oils through the three-way valve, controlled by the engine control system - in Auto mode the engine control system selects automatically between the two grades according to the engine's control configuration; High BN and Low BN modes use that grade only - and fails safe to the high-BN oil. The maker shows the valve either on the ship side ahead of one heating tank or, on GI engines, on the engine behind separate low-BN and high-BN inlets. The maker describes it as securing fully acceptable conditions where a longer changeover period is available.

ACOM Mk III - automated cylinder oil mixing (an option for engines that burn high-sulphur fuel; not applicable to low-sulphur-only engines). It mixes two fully formulated cylinder oils in a small tank to the BN that the control system orders from the fuel sulphur, giving a faster change of BN. Since Category II BN 40 oils became available, the maker no longer recommends mixing for low-sulphur operation.

blocks.p: Neither system meters the oil or sets the feed rate - the Alpha lubricator and its control do that. BN selection and feed rate are separate control decisions: the supply system decides how much alkali each drop carries; the lubricator control decides how many drops arrive. The maker's name for the feed control is Alpha ACC (Adaptive, or Adaptable, Cylinder oil Control); its sulphur-proportional factor is now called the feed-rate factor.

Dual-fuel operation on this engine. The maker uses the same low-BN oil for LNG, ethane, LPG or methanol as for fuel of up to 0.50% sulphur, so a change between gas and low-sulphur fuel does not by itself require a change of oil. The crew enters the pilot fuel's sulphur, and the control system calculates a 'sulphur equivalent' from engine load, pilot-fuel quantity and pilot sulphur. A higher-BN oil is needed only when high-sulphur fuel is burnt.

A different maker. WinGD's Pulse Jet system uses one servo-oil-operated pump per cylinder under the engine control system, with tailored spray angles and most of the oil placed above the ring pack; its optional automatic grade changeover is the iCAT. Never transfer one maker's settings to the other.
Full-size diagrams: D3 - ACOS2 automated cylinder oil switching; D4 - ACOM Mk III automated cylinder oil mixing; D6 - WinGD Pulse Jet (a different maker).

The question is two questions joined by 'and'. Splitting it into steps 1 to 3 (the system) and steps 4 to 7 (the optimisation) makes the balance visible while writing, which matters because the sketch is seductive - it is easy to spend twenty minutes drawing and then write three lines on sulphur. The sketch should be a labelled line diagram, not a work of art. Steps 1 to 7 are the core examination answer. Step 8 is a separately labelled technical extension: it earns credit on a 'new generation' question, but write it only once steps 1 to 7 are secure.
Step 2 is written as a numbered list precisely so it doubles as the sketch's label list. Draw the diagram, number the components, and the description writes itself.

Historical and current context. This question was set in essentially the same words in March 2022 and February 2024 (QP2203 Q9, QP2402 Q4). The answers written for those sittings, MIW's QP2402 Q4 included, present the sulphur-proportional ACC factor as the general rule for setting the feed. The maker's guidance since June 2023 confines that factor to high-sulphur fuel. Write to the current guidance and say that you are doing so.

Alkali delivered equals base number times quantity. Everything in the second half of the answer comes out of that one relation. It explains why there are two knobs and not one; why a high-BN oil at low feed and a low-BN oil at higher feed can be equivalent; why the sulphur percentage must be entered by hand from the bunker delivery note; and why the answer to low-sulphur fuel is a different grade rather than simply less oil. On a modern engine the two knobs are two different pieces of equipment: the supply system (ACOS2 switching or ACOM mixing) decides the BN reaching the lubricator, and the lubricator control decides the quantity.

blocks.h: The named engine in detail - Everllence B&W G95ME-C10.5-GI

blocks.p: The maker's current project guide for the G95ME-C10.5-GI (July 2026) describes the arrangement drawn in D1. Points worth knowing beyond the examination minimum:

ul: Drive and control. The Alpha lubricator is mounted on each cylinder's hydraulic cylinder unit (HCU), which is supplied with 300 bar system oil from the engine's hydraulic power supply. That hydraulic supply is separate from the cylinder oil: the lubricator's own small multi-piston pumps meter the cylinder oil and inject it to the quills. The maker's current documents do not state what medium actuates those pumps, so it is not stated here. The Cylinder Control Unit of the engine control system triggers it through a solenoid valve - a proportional valve on the Alpha Mk 2 - and reads a feedback sensor; a level switch watches the oil supply. Because the ME engine control system runs it, the maker also calls it the 'ME lubricator'. See D2 - Alpha lubricator control and injection (functional blocks).

Variants. The project guide shows pipe arrangements for both the Alpha/ME lubricator and the Alpha Mk 2, which the maker describes as having improved injection flexibility; the Mk 2 can deliver one or several timed injections per revolution. The guide does not state which of the two is standard on this engine.

MC/MC-C engines are different. Older camshaft engines with Alpha lubricators use a separate pump station and a stand-alone controller (the ALCU, now replaced by the ALCU 2R), and their lubricators carry accumulators that must be kept charged. Do not describe those items as part of an ME engine's system.

Supply side. The project guide shows the standard ACOS2 in two layouts, which should not be mixed. In the section for all engines (Fig. 9.01.01) the switching valve sits on the ship side, ahead of a filter and one heating tank, with a single engine inlet (AC) - the layout drawn in D1. In the section for GI engines (Figs. 9.02.02a and 9.02.04a) each oil has its own filter, small heated tank and pipe to the engine - low BN to inlet AC1, high BN to AC2 - and the ACOS valve on the engine selects between them; the maker marks this 'ACOS (not SDF)', and with ACOM (SDF) the engine has a single inlet. Either way the whole line to the engine is insulated and electrically heat-traced. In Auto mode the engine control system selects between the two grades automatically according to the engine's control configuration; the maker's published Auto-mode rule is not reproduced (see Uncertainty). The maker says ACOM removes the need for two cylinder oil service/day tanks and for the heating tank; its own small heated tanks are fed by gravity from the storage tanks. See D3 - ACOS2 automated cylinder oil switching and D4 - ACOM Mk III automated cylinder oil mixing.
Load changes. The control raises the feed temporarily during starting, manoeuvring and load changes (load-change-dependent lubrication), and can pre-lubricate the cylinders before starting.

blocks.h: Dual-fuel operation on the named engine

blocks.p: The maker's current guidance uses the same cylinder oil for LNG, ethane, LPG and methanol as for fuel oil of up to 0.50% sulphur - a Category II BN 40 oil on Mark 9 and later engines and on dual-fuel engines - so moving between gas and low-sulphur fuel does not by itself require a change of oil. In dual-fuel mode the control system calculates a 'sulphur equivalent' from engine load, the amount of pilot fuel and the pilot fuel's sulphur, which the crew enters on the operating panel. A higher-BN oil (BN 100-140+, or an ACOM mix) is needed only for high-sulphur fuel. The maker's ammonia-engine project guide gives no ammonia-specific cylinder-oil guidance, so none is offered here. WinGD's guideline states only that no high-BN oil is required on LNG, methanol or ammonia. Do not assume one maker's dual-fuel oil rule applies to another maker's engine.

blocks.h: Switching, mixing, blending and metering - four different jobs

blocks.p: ACOS2 switches between two finished oils. ACOM mixes two fully formulated cylinder oils in a small unit on the supply line, to a BN that the engine control system orders from the fuel sulphur. Blending on board is a third, separately installed approach and not an Everllence system: the SEA-Mate Blending-on-Board (BOB) unit, originally developed by A.P. Moller-Maersk and now supplied by Marine Fluid Technology, blends the engine's in-use system oil - or a low-BN cylinder oil - with a high-BN cylinder-oil product to a set BN and fills a day tank, from which the oil reaches the engine by the normal supply path. WinGD's current list of validated oils includes additives intended for blending on board. None of the three meters the oil into the cylinder - on this engine the Alpha lubricator and its control do that. Which of these a particular ship carries is an installation fact: check the ship's own documents rather than assuming it from the owner or the engine type.

blocks.h: The competing maker - WinGD Pulse Jet

blocks.p: WinGD's Pulse Jet system (called the Pulse Lubricating System in WinGD's installation manuals) is a genuinely different design, not a variant of the Alpha lubricator. Each cylinder has its own lubricating pump, operated by servo oil and controlled by the engine control system through a solenoid valve, with a pressure transmitter for feedback. The quills carry non-return valves, and their spray angles and the injection timing are tailored for an even distribution; the control-system timing places the oil above, into and below the ring pack, usually mostly above it. Oil reaches the engine as a single validated grade, through two service tanks with manual changeover valves near the engine inlet, or - on engines ordered with it - through the automatic iCAT (WinGD: integrated Cylinder lubricant Auto Transfer system), controlled by the engine control system, which adds a separate high-BN engine inlet with its own filter; its change-over valve, one per cylinder near the lubricating pump and after the filters, selects the low-BN or the high-BN inlet. WinGD's guideline has the drain oil sampled at least weekly for residual BN and iron, on board and by laboratory. In its 'Safe' band the feed is reduced in steps to a stated minimum, or held. See D6 - WinGD Pulse Jet (a different maker).

ul: Describing a mechanical, camshaft-driven lubricator when the question says 'new generation'. The point of the modern system is electronic timing and metering.
Treating feed rate as the only variable and never mentioning base number.
Assuming over-lubrication is harmless. It causes deposits, bore polishing and stuck rings.
Forgetting that the sulphur figure is entered by the engineer, not measured by the engine.
Omitting the maker's minimum feed rate - the single most important operational limit in the whole answer.
Confusing cylinder oil with system oil, or suggesting cylinder oil is filtered and returned. It is total-loss.

Calling the Alpha lubricator a 'common-rail' system, or giving the ME engine's lubricator an accumulator. Neither is in the maker's description of the ME arrangement; accumulators belong to the older MC/MC-C Alpha lubricators.
Treating ACOS2 or ACOM as the lubricator. They deliver the right oil to it; the lubricator meters it.

Calling ACOM 'blending on board'. ACOM mixes two finished cylinder oils in the engine's supply system to an ordered BN; a blending-on-board unit makes cylinder oil from system oil (or a low-BN oil) and a high-BN product and fills a day tank. Different equipment, different principle.
Applying the sulphur-proportional factor on low-sulphur fuel. On the maker's current guidance it governs only on high-sulphur fuel; otherwise the minimum feed-rate setting does.
Quoting a feed rate or BN figure as if it were universal. Name the maker and say the figures come from its current service letter for that engine; do not transfer them to another maker.

'You have reduced the feed rate and iron in the scrape-down has risen. What now?' Restore the previous rate immediately, then investigate - the reduction has passed the point where the film or the alkali is adequate.
'Residual BN in the scrape-down is very high. Is that good?' No - it means alkali is being thrown away unburnt and the rate is above what the fuel needs.
'Why not just run maximum feed always?' Cost, deposits, bore polishing, stuck rings and higher emissions of unburnt oil.

'What happens on entering an ECA?' The fuel changes to 0.10% sulphur and the sulphur entry must be changed with it. On an engine already running a low-BN oil for 0.50% fuel, the maker's guidance does not call for a change of oil; a change of grade is needed when the ship moves between high-sulphur fuel and low-sulphur fuel.

'The ship has ACOM. Why not order one mid-range BN all the time?' Because the BN should follow the fuel's sulphur. For low-sulphur fuel the maker now recommends a single Category II BN 40 oil rather than a mixture.
'Is the ACC factor still how the feed is set?' Only on high-sulphur fuel, where the maker now calls it the feed-rate factor. On low-sulphur fuel and gas the minimum feed-rate setting governs.
Being asked for numbers. State the principle and the basis, and say that the actual figures come from the engine maker's and oil supplier's current recommendation for that installation.
What is cold corrosion and where on the liner does it occur? Corrosive wear from condensed sulphuric acid where the wall is below the acid dew point, typically in the upper part of the liner.
What is bore polishing and why does it matter? Loss of the honed surface pattern, so the liner no longer retains oil - it follows over-lubrication and deposit build-up.
How many quills per liner, and why several? The number depends on the engine type; several round the circumference so that oil reaches the whole ring pack in the time available.
What does iron in the scrape-down tell you? Wear rate, and the form of the iron indicates the wear mechanism.
Where does the cylinder oil finally go? Burnt with the charge, or scraped down to the scavenge drain.
What does the ACOS2 valve do if control air or its signal is lost? A spring returns it to the high-BN oil.

What is a 'sulphur equivalent'? The sulphur content of the fuel actually burnt in dual-fuel operation, which the control system calculates from engine load, the amount of pilot fuel and the pilot fuel's sulphur.

What triggers and meters the Alpha lubricator on an ME engine? The cylinder control unit commands a solenoid valve (a proportional valve on the Mk 2) that activates each stroke, and the lubricator's small multi-piston pumps meter and inject the cylinder oil. It is mounted on the hydraulic cylinder unit, which is supplied with 300 bar system oil, but the maker's current documents do not state the medium that actuates the lubricator - say so rather than guess.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the cylinder lubricating system question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the oil must do and why it is once-through. 2 The layout to sketch level. 3 How the dose is timed and controlled. 4 Why sulphur drives base number and quantity. 5 Setting the optimum feed rate. 6 Verifying it. 7 The traps. Then 8, the technical extension: grade switching or mixing, dual-fuel operation, the other maker.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 7 are the core examination answer - sketch-and-describe, then sulphur. Step 8 is credit on top, written last.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the components a cylinder lubricating system sketch must show for the named engine, in oil-path order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Low-BN and high-BN oil tanks; ACOS2 switching valve (or ACOM Mk III mixer); filter; heating tank with low-level alarm; insulated heat-traced pipe and main pipe, with an open/closed supply valve to each lubricator; Alpha lubricator on each HCU (the HCU is supplied with 300 bar system oil), whose multi-piston pumps meter the cylinder oil, each stroke triggered by a solenoid or proportional valve; several quills per liner with non-return valves; cylinder control unit with feedback sensor; scavenge drain for sampling.
retrieval_cards.why: This list is both the sketch labels and the description - draw it, number it, describe it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a new-generation lubricator differ from a mechanical one?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is electronically timed and independently metered. The control unit injects a measured quantity through non-return valves as the piston rings pass the quills on the upstroke, intermittently - for instance every 2, 4 or 8 revolutions - setting the frequency from engine speed and fuel index. The dose therefore follows load, fuel sulphur and oil BN, not a mechanical drive.
retrieval_cards.why: The question says 'new generation'; describing a camshaft-driven lubricator answers a different question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain cold corrosion and the role of base number.
retrieval_cards.answer: Sulphur burns to SO2 and SO3. Where the liner wall is below the acid dew point, water vapour condenses and the oxides dissolve to form sulphuric acid on the liner, corroding liner and rings. The cylinder oil carries an overbased alkaline reserve, measured as its Base Number, which neutralises that acid.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanism, not the slogan. Everything about grade selection follows from it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is over-lubrication not the safe option?
retrieval_cards.answer: Excess alkaline oil forms hard calcium deposits on the piston top land and in the ring grooves, causes bore polishing which destroys the liner's oil-retaining honing pattern, sticks rings, increases cost and increases emission of unburnt oil.
retrieval_cards.why: The most common wrong assumption on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you optimise the feed rate downward safely, and how do you prove it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Choose the BN grade for the fuel in use and enter the sulphur from the bunker delivery note. On high-sulphur fuel the feed follows the feed-rate factor times sulphur; on low-sulphur fuel and gas the minimum feed-rate setting governs. Reduce in small steps only after good condition and acceptable drain-oil iron are confirmed, holding between steps. Prove it by residual BN and iron, scavenge port inspection, daily consumption checks and liner wear.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the marks-bearing operating procedure and the part that shows shipboard judgement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Scrape-down residual base number is very high. What does it mean and what do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Alkali is being delivered in excess of what the fuel's sulphur requires and is being wasted. Provided iron content and liner condition are satisfactory and the maker's minimum is respected, the feed rate can be reduced in a controlled step and the result monitored before any further reduction.
retrieval_cards.why: Tests whether the candidate can interpret the analysis rather than merely name it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between ACOS2 and ACOM on an Everllence B&W engine?
retrieval_cards.answer: ACOS2 SWITCHES between two cylinder oils through a three-way valve controlled by the engine control system, and fails safe to the high-BN oil; it is the standard system and suits a longer changeover period. ACOM Mk III MIXES two fully formulated oils to the BN ordered from the fuel sulphur, for a faster change; it is an option for high-sulphur operation. Neither meters the oil - the Alpha lubricator does.
retrieval_cards.why: Switching, mixing and metering are three different jobs; examiners reward keeping them apart.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On a current MAN/Everllence engine, when does the feed-rate factor (the old ACC factor) actually set the feed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only on high-sulphur fuel, where the feed is the factor times the sulphur percentage, never below the minimum. On fuel of up to 0.50% sulphur and on gas or methanol the product falls below the minimum, so the minimum feed-rate setting governs and is optimised from inspection and drain-oil results.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest out-of-date statement in answers to this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A G95ME-GI engine changes from very-low-sulphur fuel oil to gas mode. Must the cylinder oil be changed?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not on the maker's current guidance - the same low-BN Category II oil serves gas and fuel of up to 0.50% sulphur. The pilot fuel's sulphur must still be entered so that the system can calculate the sulphur equivalent. A change of oil is needed when moving to or from high-sulphur fuel.
retrieval_cards.why: Tests whether the candidate knows the dual-fuel position rather than assuming every fuel change means a grade change.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where is the oil placed by an Everllence B&W Alpha system, compared with a WinGD Pulse Jet system?
retrieval_cards.answer: Alpha: injected through non-return valves as the piston rings pass the quills on the upstroke - into the ring pack. WinGD Pulse Jet: jets with tailored spray angles, placed by control-system timing above, into and below the ring pack - usually mostly above it. Different makers, different logic; never transfer settings between them.
retrieval_cards.why: Shows the candidate has named a make and knows it is not the only design.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Cylinder oil: film, neutralise, clean, seal, carry debris - and it is TOTAL LOSS. Named engine: Everllence B&W G95ME-C10.5-GI. Sketch path: two BN grades, ACOS2 switching valve, filter, heating tank, heat-traced line, main pipe, Alpha lubricator on each HCU (solenoid or proportional valve; multi-piston pumps meter the cylinder oil), quills with non-return valves, cylinder control unit. Dose: timed onto the ring pack, intermittent, set from speed and fuel index. Sulphur burns to acid below the dew point, neutralised by BN. Two decisions: the grade (supply system) and the feed (lubricator control). High-sulphur fuel: factor times S%; low-sulphur fuel and gas: the minimum. Reduce in small steps; prove by drain-oil BN and iron, port inspection, consumption and wear.

questions.text_verbatim: (a) Briefly discuss the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC) and its key objectives behind the establishment of the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification for ships? (b) How does the HSSC enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of Port State Control inspections for ships? (c) What challenges or complexities are associated with the implementation of the HSSC, and how are they addressed?
questions.understand_first: The HSSC does not change what a ship must comply with. It changes WHEN she is looked at, by aligning the surveys and certificate validity of separate conventions onto one five-year cycle with one anniversary date. Every objective, every port State control benefit, and every implementation difficulty in this answer follows from that single idea - including the honest limitation that harmonising the calendar does nothing about what happens between the dates.
