blocks.h: (a) The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification
1. What the HSSC is, and the problem it solved

blocks.p: Before harmonization each convention imposed its own surveys, its own certificate validity and its own expiry date. A single ship therefore held certificates falling due at different times, and had to be surveyed on several separate occasions by several separate attendances - with the ship out of service each time. The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification aligns the survey requirements and certificate validity periods of the principal statutory instruments into one common cycle with one common anniversary date, so that the ship can be surveyed for all of them at essentially the same time.

blocks.h: 2. The instruments that carry it, and the edition in force

blocks.p: The HSSC was introduced by the 1988 Protocol to SOLAS 1974 and the 1988 Protocol to the Load Lines Convention 1966, by resolution MEPC.39(29) for MARPOL and MEPC.132(53) for MARPOL Annex VI, and by corresponding amendments to the IBC, IGC and BCH Codes; the Ballast Water Management Convention included it from the outset. The Guidelines now extend across SOLAS 74/88, the Load Lines Convention 66/88, MARPOL, the BWM Convention, the IBC, IGC and BCH Codes, the Polar Code and, since the 2025 edition, the IP Code.

The operative edition at this sitting is resolution A.1207(34), the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025, adopted 3 December 2025, which revoked A.1186(33) and takes into account amendments entering into force before or on 31 December 2025.

blocks.h: 3. The key objectives behind its establishment

ol: One survey occasion instead of many - align the surveys required by different instruments so they can be carried out together.
A common certificate cycle and anniversary date, so all statutory certificates run and expire together.
Minimise the time the ship is out of service and the commercial disruption that repeated attendances cause.
Reduce the administrative burden on Administrations, recognized organizations and shipowners alike.
Provide flexibility - a window within which a survey may be done - without lowering the standard being surveyed to.
Remove conflict and duplication between the survey requirements of different instruments, so that a single coherent regime applies.

blocks.h: 4. How the system works - survey types, cycle and time window

blocks.p: The Guidelines describe seven types of survey: initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom, and additional. The harmonized system provides for a one-year standard interval between surveys based on those types as appropriate - with the exception of MARPOL Annex IV, which is based on initial and renewal surveys only.

Certificates run for a maximum of five years on a common anniversary date. Flexibility is built in: the renewal survey may be completed within three months before the expiry date with no loss of the certificate's period of validity, and annual and intermediate surveys have a six-month time window - from three months before to three months after the anniversary date. The Guidelines also set out the conditions for extending a certificate, for revalidation, for surveys after transfer of flag, and - in this edition - for the application of remote surveys, which were brought in following the experience of the pandemic and advances in technology.

blocks.h: (b) The HSSC and port State control
5. (b) How the HSSC helps port State control

blocks.p: Efficiency - the officer meets one coherent certificate set on one anniversary date, in harmonised forms with a standard record of surveys and endorsements. The initial document check that begins every inspection is therefore faster and can be done consistently by officers in different regions. Because the endorsements are standard, an officer does not need to know each convention's separate survey vocabulary to read them.

Effectiveness - alignment makes a gap visible. If one certificate is unendorsed or a survey is overdue against its window, that stands out immediately against the others, and gives the officer clear grounds to move from a document check to a more detailed inspection under SOLAS regulation I/19 and the port State control procedures, which at this sitting are those of resolution A.1206(34), Procedures for Port State Control, 2025. It also removes the situation in which a ship was technically in order on one certificate and lapsed on another, which previously allowed genuine deficiencies to hide in the mismatch. Fewer, better-documented surveys mean the officer can target effort rather than duplicate what the flag has already verified.

blocks.h: 6. (c) The challenges and complexities of implementation

ul: Getting an existing ship onto a single anniversary date in the first place, which requires certificates to be shortened or extended and is administratively awkward.
The window may not suit the ship. A trading pattern or a drydock booking may not place the ship where a surveyor can attend within the three-month-either-side window.
Surveyor availability - the world fleet is global and recognized organizations are not equally present in every port.
Multiple recognized organizations. Where a flag delegates different certificates to different societies, the coordination the HSSC was meant to simplify returns in another form.

Keeping the Guidelines current. Nine parent instruments are amended on their own timetables, so the Guidelines themselves must be reissued repeatedly - each edition has revoked its predecessor after about two years (A.1186(33) in 2023, A.1207(34) in 2025).
Consistency of interpretation between Administrations and between recognized organizations, which determines whether the same standard is actually applied.
A survey is a snapshot. Alignment does not stop condition deteriorating between attendances.

rows: Windows that do not suit the ship
The flexibility provisions themselves - the six-month window, renewal completable three months before expiry with no loss of validity, and the Guidelines' conditions for extension and revalidation
The Assembly reissues the Guidelines regularly, and MSC and MEPC are requested to keep them under continuous review and amend them as necessary
Recognition of remote surveys in this edition, and the global surveyor networks of recognized organizations
The RO Code, which sets mandatory standards for organizations acting on a flag's behalf, together with class unified requirements and interpretations
The III Code and the mandatory IMO Member State Audit Scheme, which audit how a flag actually discharges these obligations
Continuous survey arrangements, the Enhanced Survey Programme for bulk carriers and oil tankers, and approved planned maintenance schemes, which give continuity between statutory attendances

blocks.p: The mark split is 8 + 4 + 4 and the discipline it demands is to write twice as much on limb (a) as on either of the others. Four steps for (a), one for (b) and two for (c) enforces that on the page. Limbs (b) and (c) are four marks each - roughly four or five scoring propositions apiece - and a candidate who writes an essay on port State control has taken time from limb (a) where the marks actually are.

Limb (b) asks about efficiency and effectiveness. Those are two different claims: efficiency is about the officer's time, effectiveness is about whether he catches things. Answering them under separate labels is worth doing explicitly.

Limb (c) asks two questions - what is hard, and how is it addressed. The two-column table at step 7 pairs each challenge with its answer and guarantees the second half is not forgotten, which is the usual failure.

The HSSC harmonises the CALENDAR, not the standard. It does not change what a ship must comply with; it changes when and how often she is looked at, and makes all the looking happen together. Every objective, every port State control benefit and every implementation difficulty falls out of that one sentence - including the honest limitation that aligning the calendar does nothing about what happens between the dates.

ul: Confusing intermediate and periodical surveys. They are separate types; periodical attaches to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificates.
Saying the HSSC 'raised safety standards'. It harmonised the survey calendar; the standards live in the conventions.
Giving the window as three months rather than a six-month window, three months either side of the anniversary.
Forgetting that the renewal survey may be completed three months before expiry with no loss of validity - a favourite oral question.
Naming only SOLAS and MARPOL. The Guidelines cover nine instruments including the Polar Code and the IP Code.
Answering limb (c) only on challenges and never on how they are addressed.
Quoting the wrong edition of the Guidelines. See the trap below.

The edition. The Survey Guidelines are reissued roughly every two years by Assembly resolution. At this sitting the operative edition is A.1207(34), adopted 3 December 2025 and revoking A.1186(33). Quoting A.1186(33) - the edition in the February 2024 answer - is out of date by this sitting.
Which certificate carries which survey type? Periodical surveys attach to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificates - not to all of them.
The MARPOL Annex IV exception - initial and renewal surveys only, no annual or intermediate. A neat detail that shows the text has been read.
Being asked whether a port State control officer can go beyond the certificates. Yes, on clear grounds, under SOLAS regulation I/19 and the port State control procedures.
Being asked what is new in the current edition. The application of remote surveys, following pandemic experience and advancing technology.
Name the seven survey types. Initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom, additional.
What is the anniversary date? The day and month corresponding to the expiry date of the certificate, against which the annual and intermediate windows are set.
How long is a statutory certificate valid? A maximum of five years.

What happens if the renewal survey is completed four months before expiry? It falls outside the three-month allowance, so the new certificate does not simply run from the old expiry date - the Guidelines' rules on this must be followed.
Who may carry out these surveys? The Administration, or a recognized organization acting on its behalf under the RO Code.

blocks.p: Limb (a) is What - Where - Why - How: what it is (1), which instruments carry it (2), the objectives (3), the mechanics (4). Limb (b) is two words, efficiency and effectiveness. Limb (c) is hard, then fixed. For the mechanics remember 7 types, 5 years, 1 year interval, 6-month window, 3 months before expiry.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the Assembly edition boundary

blocks.p: The single live risk on this question is the edition of the Survey Guidelines, and it was settled before writing. The 34th Assembly adopted its resolutions on 3 December 2025, so the A.12xx(34) series is operative and A.1207(34) is the correct edition; its predecessor A.1186(33) was revoked by it. A.1207(34) was read from the IMO text for this candidate on 21 September 2026: resolution paragraph 4 revokes A.1186(33), annex section 1.1 lists nine instruments (the IP Code added), and section 1.3 carries the same one-year interval, six-month window and three-month renewal rule as the 2023 edition. SOLAS regulation I/19 is cited by number for the control power; no licensed IMO consolidated SOLAS edition is held in the corpus, so its wording rests on authoritative secondary reproduction, and that limitation is recorded rather than concealed. No certificate-extension period beyond the three-month renewal allowance and the six-month window is quoted, because the Guidelines' extension conditions are conditional and quoting a bare number would flatten them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the HSSC question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 What it is and the problem it solved. 2 The instruments carrying it and the edition in force. 3 The key objectives. 4 The mechanics - survey types, cycle, window. (b) 5 Efficiency and effectiveness for port State control. (c) 6 The challenges. 7 How they are addressed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the seven survey types under the HSSC and give the cycle and window.
retrieval_cards.answer: Initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom, and additional. Certificates run a maximum of five years on a common anniversary date, with a one-year standard interval between surveys. Annual and intermediate surveys have a six-month window - three months before to three months after the anniversary. The renewal survey may be completed within three months before expiry with no loss of the certificate's period of validity.
retrieval_cards.why: The mechanics carry most of limb (a)'s eight marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution is the operative HSSC edition, and what did it replace?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1207(34), the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025, adopted 3 December 2025, which revoked A.1186(33) and takes into account amendments entering into force before or on 31 December 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: The edition is the live temporal boundary on this question and the easiest way to date an answer wrongly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the key objectives behind establishing the HSSC.
retrieval_cards.answer: Align the surveys required by different instruments so one occasion serves all; give all statutory certificates a common cycle and anniversary date; minimise out-of-service time and commercial disruption; reduce administrative burden on Administrations, ROs and owners; provide flexibility through survey windows without lowering the standard; and remove conflict and duplication between instruments.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) explicitly asks for the objectives, and they are pure marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the HSSC make port State control more efficient AND more effective?
retrieval_cards.answer: Efficient - one coherent certificate set on one anniversary date, in harmonised forms with standard endorsements, so the opening document check is faster and consistent between regions. Effective - alignment makes a missing endorsement or an overdue survey stand out against the others, giving clear grounds to escalate under SOLAS regulation I/19 and the procedures of A.1206(34), and removing the mismatch in which a ship was in order on one certificate and lapsed on another.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) names both properties; they are different claims and must be answered separately.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give three implementation challenges of the HSSC and how each is addressed.
retrieval_cards.answer: Windows that do not suit the trading pattern - addressed by the flexibility provisions themselves, the six-month window and the extension and revalidation rules. Keeping the Guidelines current across eight amending instruments - addressed by regular Assembly reissue with MSC and MEPC keeping them under review. Inconsistent recognized organization performance - addressed by the RO Code and class unified requirements, with the III Code and the Member State Audit Scheme auditing the flag itself.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) has two halves and candidates routinely answer only the first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Did the HSSC raise safety standards?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It harmonised the survey calendar and certificate validity across instruments. The standards themselves remain in the conventions. Harmonisation also does nothing about deterioration between surveys, which is why continuous survey arrangements, the Enhanced Survey Programme and approved planned maintenance schemes exist alongside it.
retrieval_cards.why: Understanding what the HSSC does NOT do is the mark that separates a good answer from a recitation.

Now: one common anniversary, one five-year cycle, seven survey types - initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, bottom inspection, additional - on a one-year standard interval, with a six-month window three months either side of the anniversary and renewal completable three months before expiry with no loss of validity. Operative edition A.1207(34), 3 December 2025, revoking A.1186(33). For PSC: efficiency from one coherent certificate set, effectiveness because gaps become visible and give clear grounds.

questions.text_verbatim: An Indian flag vessel has grounded off the coast of India, and the owners have abandoned the property. In accordance with the provisions under the Merchant Shipping Act, what steps should be initiated and who should initiate such steps for the safety of the ships and the marine environment.
questions.short_title: Grounded and Abandoned Indian Flag Vessel - Action under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025
questions.understand_first: The question names 'the Merchant Shipping Act' without a year. At September 2026 that means the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, in force as a whole from 15 March 2026. The examiner is testing whether you can show that abandonment moves the initiative to the State without moving the liability off the owner - and name who acts: master, Director-General of Maritime Administration, the nodal authority, Coast Guard, receiver of wreck, Central Government. The response powers of Part X are now worked out in the Merchant Shipping (Marine Incident and Emergency Response) Rules, 2026 (G.S.R. 354(E), in force from their Gazette publication on 12 May 2026).

blocks.h: 1. The statute, and what abandonment changes

blocks.p: At the date of this examination the governing statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act 24 of 2025). It received assent on 18 August 2025 and the Central Government, by notification S.O. 1244(E) dated 10 March 2026, brought its provisions into force on 15 March 2026. Section 324(1) repeals the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (except its Part XIV, not including section 411A), and section 324(2) saves appointments, orders and pending proceedings. Four Parts of the 2025 Act engage on these facts:

headers: What it gives on these facts
rows: Prevention and containment of pollution from vessel and response
Reporting, notice to the owner, direct action by the Central Government, cost recovery - and an express rule for an ABANDONED vessel

A notified nodal authority, the owner, master and seafarers as primary response party, powers of direction and requisition - worked out in the Merchant Shipping (Marine Incident and Emergency Response) Rules, 2026 (G.S.R. 354(E))
Investigation and inquiries on marine casualties
A vessel stranded or abandoned on or near the coast is a marine casualty for investigation
Receiver of wreck, hazard determination, marking and removal at the owner's cost, compulsory insurance, salvage

blocks.p: What abandonment changes, and what it does not. When the owners walk away, the practical initiative passes to the State. It does not end the owner's liability: the Act lets the authorities act and then recover the cost from the owner, charges it on the owner's other ships, and allows claims directly against the insurer.

blocks.h: 2. Immediate action - life first, then report

ul: Safety of life comes first. While anyone remains on board, the master and seafarers are, with the owner, the primary response party (s.226(1)) and must comply with the nodal authority's directions (s.226(2)). The Indian Coast Guard coordinates search and rescue.

Report the casualty. Where a maritime casualty results in a wreck, the master, owner or operator must report it without delay to the Director-General - under the 2025 Act the Director-General of Maritime Administration (s.2; appointed under s.7), successor to the Director-General of Shipping - and to the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre or Sub-Centre of the Indian Coast Guard (s.236(1)).
Report pollution. Where oil or other harmful substances escape, or are likely to, the master must report the incident (s.138(1)).
Contain on board while the crew remain: sound tanks, assess hull damage, stop leaks, transfer oil away from damaged tanks where safe, and prevent the ship working further on the ground.

blocks.h: 3. The pollution powers - Part VII, section 138

blocks.p: This is the provision that answers the question most directly where the owner has abandoned the ship.

ol: Notice to the owner (s.138(2)). On receiving the report the Central Government may serve notice on the owner, agent, master, charterer, operator, lessee or licensee to: prevent the escape of harmful substances; remove the cargo or oil; move the vessel; clean up slicks; prohibit removal of the vessel or her cargo; and take any other necessary action.

The abandoned-vessel rule (s.138(3)). If the vessel is abandoned, or her report is incomplete, the Central Government fixes responsibility for the incident on the master or owner. Abandonment therefore does not dissolve responsibility; the Act assigns it.

Direct action (s.138(4) and (5)). Where there is grave and imminent danger to the coast or coastal waters, or where a notice is not complied with, the Central Government may itself take the measures needed to prevent, mitigate or eliminate the threat. On these facts - owners gone - this is the operative power.

Cost recovery (s.138(6)). The expenditure is a debt due to the Central Government, recoverable from the persons served, and a charge on any vessel they own, which may be detained and, if the debt is not paid, sold.
Other vessels (s.139). The Government may, by written order, direct the owner of any Indian vessel or equipment to provide services or assistance.

blocks.p: Operationally the oil spill response is run under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan, with the Indian Coast Guard as coordinating authority for response at sea.

blocks.h: 4. Emergency response - Part X and the MIER Rules 2026

ul: The Central Government appoints by notification one or more nodal authorities to administer and supervise marine incidents and the maritime emergency response (s.225). No s.225 notification was located as at 21 September 2026. The Directorate General of Maritime Administration describes itself as the national nodal authority, but the Act requires a notification, so the answer names the office by its statutory description.
The nodal authority may issue written directions to Central and State bodies, requisition officers, and requisition pollution response equipment (s.228).

The Merchant Shipping (Marine Incident and Emergency Response) Rules, 2026, G.S.R. 354(E) of 12 May 2026, made under s.230 read with s.228(4), are in force from their publication in the Gazette. The nodal authority must coordinate and supervise the response and may issue directions to the master, owner, managers, salvors, insurers, ports and others - including removal or containment of hazards and pollution control (r.3(1)-(3)). Where directions fail it may enter premises, assume control of the ship and arrange salvage and pollution response itself (r.3(4)). For an abandoned ship the decisive rule is r.4(1): the nodal authority must initiate immediate response where the primary response party delays or is unable to act, and may hand control back once that party is ready (r.4(2)). The Director-General ensures overall coordination of all responders and communicates with the owner and the flag, port and coastal States (r.3(6)); the Principal Officer enforces compliance (r.3(5)). Costs incurred by those complying with directions, by affected landowners and by the Government are recoverable from the ship owner (r.5).
Every owner of an Indian vessel must maintain insurance or other financial security for liability under this Part and carry evidence of it on board (s.229).

blocks.h: 5. The wreck regime - Part XII, Chapter I

ul: Receiver of wreck (s.235). Appointed by notification to take possession of wreck, give notices, enforce the obligations of the owner, operator or insurer, and act to remove the wreck by the most practical and expeditious means consistent with safety and the marine environment.

Hazard (ss.234 and 237). The Central Government decides whether the wreck is a hazard - a danger or impediment to navigation, or a threat of major harm to the marine environment, coastline or related interests - against listed criteria including the oil on board, proximity to shipping routes, protected areas and ports.
Marking (s.238). The owner or operator must mark a hazardous wreck at his own cost and keep it marked until removed.

Removal (s.242). The Central Government informs and consults the flag State and the registered owner; the registered owner or operator must remove a hazardous wreck (s.242(3)) and produce evidence of insurance (s.242(4)); a removal plan is submitted and approved with a time limit (s.242(5)-(6)). If the owner does not remove it in time - or where immediate action is needed - the Government or the receiver removes it at the owner's expense (s.242(7)-(8)).

Liability and insurance (ss.243 and 244). The registered owner is liable for the cost of locating, marking and removing the wreck, subject to narrow defences (war or exceptional natural phenomenon, third-party intent, negligence of the authority maintaining navigational aids), and may limit liability under s.162. Indian vessels of 300 GT and above must carry compulsory insurance, and a claim may be brought directly against the insurer.

Owner's claim and time limit (ss.245 and 246). An owner may reclaim wreck or proceeds within one year on paying salvage and charges; cost-recovery claims must be made within three years of the hazard determination and six years of the casualty.

blocks.h: 6. Salvage, place of refuge and investigation

ul: Salvage. Part XII Chapter II applies to salvage operations within India's territory including coastal waters (s.247). Where a wreck-removal measure amounts to salvage, the salvage provisions apply (s.242(9)). With the owner gone, the State may have to procure salvage itself and recover the cost.

Place of refuge. A request to move the ship to sheltered water is assessed under the Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, resolution A.1184(33). A coastal State is under no obligation in international law to grant one.

Investigation. A vessel lost, abandoned, stranded or materially damaged on or near the coast of India is a marine casualty for the purposes of Part XI (s.231(1)(a)), as is pollution or its threat in coastal waters (s.231(1)(f)). Separately, the marine safety investigation follows the Casualty Investigation Code (MSC.255(84)), which seeks to prevent recurrence and does not apportion blame.

rows: Safety of life, damage assessment, immediate containment; reports under ss.138(1) and 236(1)
Salvage, marking and removal, funding - has abandoned, but responsibility is fixed on him (s.138(3)) and costs are recoverable (ss.138(6), 243)

Notice under s.138(2); direct action and cost recovery under s.138(4)-(6); hazard determination and removal orders under ss.237 and 242; investigation under Part XI; overall coordination of responders under the MIER Rules (r.3(6))
Search and rescue via MRCC/MRSC; coordination of oil spill response at sea under the national contingency plan
Supervision of the maritime emergency response, directions and requisitions (ss.225, 228); directions, intervention and immediate response where the owner cannot act (MIER Rules rr.3-4)
Custody of wreck, notices, enforcement against owner and insurer, removal (ss.235, 241, 242(8))
Navigational safety - warnings, marking and clearance where the wreck obstructs the approach
In practice funds salvage, removal and pollution response; reachable by direct action (s.244(5))

blocks.p: The order of action is: life, then pollution, then the ship and cargo, then the wreck and navigational safety, then investigation and cost recovery.

blocks.h: Why this answer changed from the February 2024 version

blocks.p: This question was set, word for word, in February 2024 (QP2402-Q8). That answer was correct for its sitting and was built on the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - Part XA (ss.356J-356L) and Part XIII (ss.390-404). None of those section numbers is usable in September 2026. The 2025 Act commenced on 15 March 2026 and s.324(1) repealed the 1958 Act (save its Part XIV). The engineering and response logic carries over; every statutory citation had to be rebuilt from the 2025 text.

Section 138(3): if the vessel is abandoned, the Central Government fixes responsibility on the master or owner. It is the Act's own answer to the word 'abandoned' in the question, and it is new in form compared with the 1958 scheme.

ul: Citing 1958 section numbers. ss.356J-356L and 390-404 belong to a repealed Act. Name the 2025 Act.
Saying abandonment ends the owner's liability. It does not - ss.138(3), 138(6), 243 and 244 all keep it on the owner and the insurer.
Forgetting the insurer. Compulsory insurance and direct action (s.244(5)) are what actually pay for a wreck removal.
Confusing the two investigations. The Part XI inquiry and the Casualty Investigation Code safety investigation have different purposes.

Naming the nodal authority without authority. s.225 provides for one or more notified nodal authorities. The Directorate's own casualty page describes it as the national nodal authority, but no s.225 Gazette notification was located, so say 'the nodal authority notified under s.225 (the Directorate describes itself as the national nodal authority)' rather than asserting a notification.

blocks.h: Treaty context (not what the question asks)

blocks.p: Chapter I of Part XII defines 'Convention' as the Nairobi Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 (s.234(b)). India is a Contracting State: accession deposited 23 March 2011, in force for India 14 April 2015 (IMO Status of Treaties, 26 August 2026). The question asks about the Act, so the Convention is context, not the answer.

Statutory text and commencement were read in the Gazette copy published by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways and are stated as at 21 September 2026. The Merchant Shipping (Marine Incident and Emergency Response) Rules, 2026 were notified as G.S.R. 354(E) in the Gazette of India Extraordinary of 12 May 2026 and are in force from that publication (rule 1(2)); they were read in the Gazette text. An earlier Ministry draft of these Rules carried a 24-hour reporting limit and a 'competent authority' definition - neither appears in the notified Rules, so do not quote them. No Gazette notification appointing a nodal authority under s.225 was located.

The question asks two things - WHAT steps and WHO initiates them. The table in step 7 answers 'who' in one glance; steps 2 to 6 answer 'what' in the order an examiner expects: life, report, pollution, emergency response, wreck, salvage, investigation.

ul: Writing the 1958 Act from memory.
Listing powers without saying who holds them.
Ignoring abandonment - the one word that makes this question different from any grounding.
Leaving out the insurer.
What does s.138(3) say? - abandoned vessel: responsibility fixed on master or owner.
Who decides whether a wreck is a hazard? - the Central Government (s.237), whose decision is final in a dispute (s.242(3) proviso).
Can the owner limit liability for wreck removal? - yes, under s.162, subject to s.243.
Who do you report a wreck to? - the Director-General and the ICG MRCC/MRSC (s.236(1)).

Who acts first if the owner has abandoned the ship? - the nodal authority initiates immediate response where the primary response party delays or cannot act (MIER Rules r.4(1)), and the cost is recoverable from the ship owner (r.5).

blocks.h: (a) The IMO and ILO human element regimes
1. (a) The human element, and how IMO and ILO divide the work

blocks.p: IMO's own term is the human element, and resolution A.947(23) treats it as a complex multi-dimensional issue affecting maritime safety, security and marine environmental protection, involving the entire spectrum of human activity - ships' crews, shore-based management, regulatory bodies, recognized organizations, shipyards and legislators. It is not simply 'crew error'.

The two organisations divide the work along a clean line: IMO regulates the seafarer as an operator of the ship - competence, safe operation, fitness for duty. ILO regulates the seafarer as a worker - employment, living and working conditions, health and welfare. Together they cover the same person from two directions.

blocks.h: 2. The IMO regime - competence, safe operation and fitness for duty

ul: STCW 1978, as amended by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force 1 January 2012 - the standards of training, certification and watchkeeping. Regulation I/6 on training and assessment, I/14 on company responsibilities, and chapter VIII with section A-VIII/1 on fitness for duty and minimum hours of rest.
The ISM Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX - safety management, dealt with in limb (b).
Resolution A.1047(27), Principles of Minimum Safe Manning - the framework by which an Administration determines the manning a ship must carry.
MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, of 24 January 2019, which address fatigue across the whole system rather than only on board.
Resolution A.947(23), the human element vision, principles and goals, which is the policy statement underlying all of the above.
The III Code and the mandatory Member State Audit Scheme, which audit whether a flag State actually gives effect to these obligations.

blocks.h: 3. The ILO regime - MLC 2006, the fourth pillar

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 consolidated a large body of earlier ILO maritime instruments and is called the fourth pillar of international maritime regulation, alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW. Its structure is distinctive: Articles and Regulations setting out the obligations, and a Code in two parts - Part A, mandatory Standards, and Part B, Guidelines to which due consideration must be given.

It is arranged in five Titles: 1 minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship; 2 conditions of employment; 3 accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; 4 health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection; and 5 compliance and enforcement.

Title 5 is what makes it real. A ship carries a Maritime Labour Certificate and a Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance - Part I drawn up by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner and certified by the authority or an authorised recognized organization - and is subject to flag State inspection, port State control, and on-board and onshore complaint procedures.

The position at this sitting. In force: the 2014 amendments (18 January 2017, financial security for repatriation and shipowners' liability), 2016 (8 January 2019), 2018 (26 December 2020) and 2022 (23 December 2024). The 2025 amendments - approved by the International Labour Conference in June 2025, on shore leave, protection against violence and harassment, and recognition of seafarers as key workers - are adopted but not yet in force. On the IMO side, a comprehensive review of STCW is in progress.

blocks.h: 4. Where the two organisations act together

ul: Medical fitness - joint IMO/ILO guidelines on medical examinations of seafarers, where the STCW medical certificate and the MLC health requirements meet.
Fair treatment of seafarers in the event of a maritime accident - joint guidelines addressing detention and criminalisation.
Abandonment of seafarers, addressed jointly and reflected in the MLC financial security requirements.

Hours of rest is the clearest overlap: STCW section A-VIII/1 sets rest hours for watchkeeping safety, and MLC Title 2 sets hours of work and rest as a labour standard. The two must be read together, and where they differ the more demanding applies.

blocks.h: (b) The human factor and the ISM Code
5. (b) The ISM Code - what it is actually trying to do

blocks.p: The ISM Code exists because a series of casualties were traced not to defective equipment but to defective management - unclear responsibility, commercial pressure on the master, and shore organisations that did not know what was happening on their own ships. The Code therefore regulates a system, not a component. Its objectives are to ensure safety at sea, prevention of human injury or loss of life, and avoidance of damage to the environment; and to that end it requires safeguards against all identified risks and continuous improvement of the safety management skills of personnel ashore and aboard.
That is why the human factor is not one topic within the Code - it is what the Code is made of. A safety management system is a set of human commitments written down.

blocks.h: 6. Where the human factor decides whether the Code works

headers: The human decision it depends on
rows: Whether responsibility and authority are genuinely defined and communicated, or exist only on an organogram
Whether the DPA truly has direct access to the highest level of management. The DPA exists specifically to bypass a hierarchy that might otherwise suppress bad news
Whether the master's overriding authority to take decisions with respect to safety and pollution prevention and to request the Company's assistance is real under commercial pressure, or nominal
Qualified, certificated and medically fit crew; proper familiarisation before taking up duties; and a common working language so that instructions are actually understood
Whether drills are treated as training or as a record to be signed
9 - Reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences
Whether people will actually report. This is the element on which the Code's capacity to learn entirely depends
Whether critical equipment is honestly identified under 10.3 rather than defined narrowly to reduce work
Whether internal audit is used to find problems or to demonstrate that there are none

blocks.h: 7. Why implementation fails, and what makes it succeed

blocks.p: Where it fails:

ul: Paper compliance. Checklists completed in advance, drills recorded but not run - the documentation is in order and the practice is not.
A system the crew do not own. An SMS written by an outside consultant, in a register the users do not read comfortably, describing a ship's operation that its own crew would not recognise.
Documentation overload. Excessive paperwork consumes the very hours the rest-hour rules protect, and fatigue then degrades the operation the system was meant to make safe.
Blame culture. If a report produces punishment, reporting stops - and element 9, the Code's learning mechanism, dies quietly while the certificate remains valid.
A DPA without independence, or a master whose overriding authority is understood by everyone to be career-limiting to use.
Familiarisation skipped on short crew turnarounds, and language barriers on multinational crews.

blocks.p: What makes it succeed:

ul: A just culture that separates honest error from wilful violation, so that near-miss reporting is safe and therefore happens.
A proportionate system, written for the ship and in the users' working language, that the crew recognise as their own.
Visible leadership - the master and Chief Engineer using the system themselves, and the Company demonstrably accepting a safety decision that costs money.
A closed feedback loop, so crews see their reports produce change. Nothing sustains reporting like evidence that reporting works.
Management review that acts on trends rather than closing findings individually - which is where the latent organisational failures are caught, as distinct from the active failures at the sharp end.

blocks.p: In short: the ISM Code can require a system, but only people can make it a real one. That is how the human factor plays its role in implementation.

Limb (a) is a broad overview - breadth and correct attribution, not depth. Four short steps with named instruments earn the eight marks; two paragraphs on STCW rest hours do not. Limb (b) is worth the same eight marks and is the harder half, because it asks for analysis. Listing the twelve elements is not analysis. Steps 6 and 7 do the analytical work by tying each element to the human decision it depends on, and then evaluating honestly why systems fail.

IMO regulates the seafarer as an operator; ILO regulates the seafarer as a worker. That single line organises the whole of limb (a) and lets you place any instrument correctly under pressure. For limb (b): the ISM Code regulates a system, and a system is made of human commitments. Everything in the Code that works, works because someone chose to make it real.

ul: Attributing the MLC to IMO. It is an ILO Convention.
Describing MLC Part B as mandatory. Part A carries the mandatory Standards; Part B is Guidelines to which due consideration must be given.
Answering limb (b) by listing the twelve ISM elements. The question asks how the human factor plays a role in implementing the Code.
Omitting the designated person ashore and the master's overriding authority - the two most explicitly human safeguards in the Code.
Treating the ISM Code as an IMO convention. It is a Code, given mandatory force by SOLAS chapter IX.
Saying nothing about why implementation fails. The analysis marks are there.
Getting the MLC amendment position wrong for the sitting. See the trap below.

The MLC amendment position. At this sitting the amendments in force are those of 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022. The 2025 amendments have been adopted but have NOT entered into force. Saying they were in force is the specific error this question is built to catch, and 'adopted' is not 'in force'.
Who draws up the DMLC? Part I by the competent authority; Part II by the shipowner, certified by the authority or an authorised recognized organization. The two are routinely inverted.
Is the ISM Code a convention? No - a Code made mandatory by SOLAS chapter IX.
What is the DPA for? Direct access to the highest level of management, so that safety information reaches the top without passing through the people it might reflect on.

Being asked to distinguish active and latent failures. Active failures are the unsafe acts at the sharp end; latent failures are the organisational conditions lying dormant until they combine with an active failure.

Being asked what the master may do under element 5. Exercise his overriding authority and responsibility to take any action he considers in the best interests of safety and pollution prevention, and request the Company's assistance.

Name the five Titles of the MLC. Minimum requirements; conditions of employment; accommodation, recreation, food and catering; health protection, medical care, welfare and social security; compliance and enforcement.
Which ISM element covers reporting of near misses? Element 9 - non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences.
Why is a common working language required? So that instructions and safety information are actually understood - element 6.
How is fatigue addressed by the two organisations? STCW section A-VIII/1 as a watchkeeping safety standard, MLC Title 2 as a labour standard, with IMO fatigue guidance alongside.
What certificate does MLC compliance produce? The Maritime Labour Certificate with the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance.

blocks.p: Limb (a): Operator and Worker. IMO instruments are S-I-M-F - STCW, ISM, Minimum safe manning, Fatigue guidance. ILO is one Convention, five Titles, two Code parts. Limb (b): 3-4-5-6-9-12 are the human elements of the ISM Code - responsibility, designated person, master's authority, resources, reporting, review. Then fails / succeeds.

Adopted but NOT in force: the 2025 amendments, approved by the ILC on 6 June 2025; their entry into force is reported for December 2027 by secondary sources and is not asserted as a date here. The February 2024 version of this answer correctly left the 2022 amendments as not in force; for this sitting that position is reversed.

questions.text_verbatim: The steering gear of the sea going vessel in which you are a Chief Engineer, stops responding while the vessel is about to enter a foreign port. Explain the following: (a) Immediate actions you would take as Chief Engineer of the ship; (b) Long term actions you would like to take, to reduce the possibility of such incidents; (c) In the event of the vessel making contact with the jetty resulting in minor oil-spillage, the legal consequences which the vessel is liable to face.
questions.short_title: Steering Gear Failure on Port Approach - Immediate and Long-Term Action, and Liability after Jetty Contact
questions.understand_first: Three limbs, 4 + 4 + 8. Limbs (a) and (b) are engineering and management: get steering back or get the ship safe, then stop it happening again. Limb (c) carries half the marks and is legal: a contact with a jetty in a foreign port, with a small spill, exposes the ship to several independent legal consequences at once. The mark is in naming them separately.

blocks.h: (a) Immediate actions of the Chief Engineer

blocks.p: Steering has failed with the ship about to enter port, so time and sea room are short. The priorities are: the Master knows at once, the standby system is tried at once, and the ship is made safe in parallel rather than after diagnosis.

ol: Inform the Master immediately and confirm what the bridge sees - rudder angle indicator, alarms, which system was in use. The navigational decisions - stopping or reducing speed, anchoring, calling tugs, exhibiting not-under-command signals and informing the pilot and VTS - are the Master's.

Start the standby power unit and change over to the other pump and control system. Most failures are confined to one power unit, one pump or one control circuit, and the duplicated arrangement exists for exactly this.

Send an engineer to the steering flat at once. Check the alarm panel, hydraulic oil level, pump running, electrical supply and control signal. If remote control has failed, transfer to local control in the steering gear compartment with a reliable communication link to the bridge and a rudder angle indicator in view.

If both systems fail, use the emergency steering arrangement and confirm the emergency or alternative power supply is available. SOLAS chapter II-1 requires, for larger rudder stocks, an alternative power supply that comes on automatically within 45 seconds.

Prepare for the worst case in parallel: anchors ready forward, engine on standby with a second generator on line, tugs requested early, SOPEP equipment ready, and the time of each event logged for the report.

ul: Investigate the root cause and report it as a non-conformity or hazardous occurrence under ISM Code element 9 - not simply 'replaced relay', but why it failed and why it was not caught.

Treat the steering gear as critical equipment under ISM element 10.3: planned maintenance of pumps, valves, control and feedback units; hydraulic oil analysis and filter condition; critical spares carried; changeover and alarm functions proven.

Make the SOLAS tests real. SOLAS regulation V/26 requires the steering gear to be checked and tested within 12 hours before departure, and emergency steering drills at least once every three months, including direct control from the steering gear compartment, the communications procedure with the bridge and, where applicable, the alternative power supply. These should exercise the full changeover, not be signed off on paper. A pre-arrival check before entering confined waters is good practice.
Train and familiarise engineers and ratings who would operate emergency steering, with posted changeover instructions in the steering flat.
Share the lesson fleet-wide through the Company and the designated person ashore, and review whether the design or maker's service information needs to be applied.

blocks.h: (c) Legal consequences of contact with the jetty and a minor spill

blocks.p: The ship is in a foreign port, so the port State's own law applies, together with the conventions that State is party to. Several consequences arise at the same time and independently of one another:

ol: Reporting and the pollution offence. The discharge must be reported to the coastal State without delay under MARPOL (Protocol I). A discharge is a MARPOL violation for which the port State may impose penalties under its own law; the defence available for a discharge resulting from damage to the ship applies only if all reasonable precautions were taken after the damage and there was no intent or recklessness.

Civil liability for pollution damage. Clean-up costs and third-party loss are claimed from the owner. If the ship is a tanker carrying oil as cargo, CLC 1992 applies where the port State is a Party; for any other ship, a spill of bunker oil falls under the Bunkers Convention 2001 where the port State is a Party. Both impose strict liability on the owner, require compulsory insurance and permit direct action against the insurer. Where the State is not a Party, its national law governs.

blocks.h: 4. Damage to the jetty and the ship's exposure

ol: Damage to the jetty. The port authority claims for repair and loss of use. The owner may be entitled to limit liability for damage to harbour works under the limitation regime applicable in that State, and the pilot's presence on board does not shift the ship's liability to the port.

Arrest and detention. The claimants may arrest the ship as security, and the port authority or port State control may detain her until the damage is surveyed, the steering gear is proven, class has attended and security - normally a P&I letter of undertaking - is provided.

Flag and class. The casualty is reported to the flag State and class; class may impose a condition of class, and the flag State may investigate. A marine safety investigation may follow under the Casualty Investigation Code.

Personal exposure of master and officers. Some States prosecute individuals for pollution offences. The IMO/ILO guidelines on fair treatment of seafarers in the event of a maritime accident bear on their treatment.
Company obligations. ISM reporting, preservation of the VDR and records, notification to P&I and hull underwriters, and cooperation with surveyors.

blocks.p: Limb (c) is worth as much as (a) and (b) together. Candidates write one paragraph on 'MARPOL fine'. The marks come from separating criminal/regulatory (report, penalty), civil (clean-up and pollution damage; jetty damage), security (arrest, detention, LOU), administrative (flag, class, investigation) and personal (master and officers).

Which liability convention applies depends on the ship and the port State, not on the ship's flag: a laden tanker is under CLC 1992 even for her bunkers; any other ship's bunker spill is under the Bunkers Convention - each only where the port State is a Party. Say this conditionally: the question does not name the port.

ul: Diagnosing before informing. The bridge must know first.
Assuming the pilot carries the liability. Pilot error does not relieve the ship of liability to third parties.
Quoting a limitation figure. Limitation amounts depend on the regime the port State applies and are not quoted here.
Treating 'minor' as 'no consequence'. Reporting is required regardless of quantity.

blocks.h: (a) Ongoing developments - technical and operational measures

blocks.p: IMO's work is framed by the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023. Its ambitions are to cut CO2 per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 against 2008; to raise zero or near-zero GHG energy to at least 5%, striving for 10%, by 2030; and to reach net-zero GHG emissions by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints of at least 20% (striving for 30%) by 2030 and at least 70% (striving for 80%) by 2040 in total annual emissions.

ul: EEDI (MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4) - a new ship's attained design index must not exceed the required value, which tightens in phases.
EEXI (regulations 23 and 25), in force 1 January 2023 - the same design approach applied once to existing ships, commonly met by engine or shaft power limitation or energy-saving devices.

SEEMP (regulation 26) in three Parts; Part III is the plan to achieve the required CII. The operative guidance is the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.395(82), as amended by MEPC.401(83) and, at MEPC 84, by MEPC.413(84); the CII calculation guidelines (G1) were amended at the same session by MEPC.412(84).

CII (regulation 28), ships of 5,000 GT and above - an annual A-to-E rating against a required value that tightens each year. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E in one year, must develop a plan of corrective actions (regulation 28.7).

Data collection system (regulation 27) - the fuel-consumption data on which every measure depends; the amendments in MEPC.385(81), in force 1 August 2025, brought enhanced data granularity from 1 January 2026.

Review of the short-term measures. The first phase of the CII/SEEMP/EEXI review was completed in 2025 and set the reduction factors to 2030; the second phase, covering the deeper questions including the metric, corrective action and enforcement, began in 2026 and is due to finish in 2028.
Life-cycle (well-to-wake) accounting under the LCA Guidelines, which underpins any fuel-based measure.
Other GHGs and new fuels - work on methane and nitrous oxide from engines, and MSC's safety framework for alternative fuels and new technologies.
The mid-term measures - see limb (b); these are the largest open item.

blocks.h: 5. What the Strategy puts in the basket

blocks.p: The 2023 Strategy calls for a basket of candidate mid-term GHG reduction measures to be developed and agreed, comprising both:

ul: a technical element - a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the marine fuel's GHG intensity; and
an economic element - a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism.

blocks.p: The two work together: the standard sets the trajectory, the price makes falling short dearer than compliance and raises revenue. Both are assessed well-to-wake and must be accompanied by a comprehensive assessment of impacts on States, with attention to developing countries, and must support a just and equitable transition. The Strategy's timetable envisaged adoption in 2025 and entry into force about 16 months later.

blocks.h: 6. The Net-Zero Framework - the basket written as draft law

blocks.p: The basket was turned into the IMO Net-Zero Framework, approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as draft amendments adding a new chapter 5 to MARPOL Annex VI. As approved in draft it would:

ul: apply to ships of 5,000 GT and above;
require an annual GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI), well-to-wake, against two tiers - a base target and a stricter direct compliance target;
require a ship that falls short to acquire remedial units (the pricing element), and let a ship that over-achieves earn surplus units;
channel revenue into an IMO Net-Zero Fund to reward low-emission ships and support a just transition.

blocks.p: The Framework is approved but NOT adopted, and nothing in it is in force. The extraordinary session convened to adopt it (MEPC/ES.2) adjourned on 17 October 2025 for one year. MEPC 84 (27 April - 1 May 2026) did not adopt it and set up an intersessional working group. IMO has announced that the extraordinary session will resume on 4 December 2026, subject to confirmation by MEPC 85 (30 November - 3 December 2026). No entry-into-force date exists. Regional schemes such as the EU Emissions Trading System are not IMO measures.

blocks.h: How this question relates to February 2024

blocks.p: Limb (a) is QP2402-Q5, word for word, but worth 8 marks instead of 16. In February 2024 'ongoing' meant: CII ratings not yet issued, basket under negotiation, nothing mid-term approved. In September 2026 the ratings are routine, the review is in its second phase, and the basket exists as an approved but unadopted Framework. Re-using the 2024 answer would describe a regulatory world that has moved on.

ul: Saying the Net-Zero Framework is adopted or in force. It is approved only. Adoption is a separate step and has not happened.
Giving a fixed adoption date. 4 December 2026 is subject to confirmation by MEPC 85; say so.
Calling the EU ETS an IMO measure. It is regional.
Saying two consecutive D ratings trigger a corrective plan. The trigger is three consecutive D ratings or one E (regulation 28.7).
